beats.lead: 1979. Atari had a policy: no game credited the person who actually built it.
beats.text: So one programmer hid his name inside the game itself.
beats.note: Warren Robinett built Adventure for the Atari 2600, and slipped in a secret room Atari never approved.

beats.text: You had to carry an almost-invisible object across the map to unlock it.
beats.note: Asked why, in his own words: "I was pissed."

beats.name: Adam Clayton
beats.role: A fifteen-year-old player who found the hidden room and mailed Atari a handwritten letter describing it, the first record of anyone outside Atari finding Robinett's secret.

beats.lead: Atari didn't have a word for what he'd done, so it made one up.
beats.text: An employee named Steve Wright coined the term "Easter egg".
beats.note: His reasoning: hiding things in games was a good thing, "like Easter eggs for players to find". The name stuck across the whole industry.

beats.text: The first hidden secret in console gaming was a protest note.

beats.line: He signed his own work because no one else would.
